ety.text: From Middle English wysard, wysarde, equivalent to wise + -ard. A uniquely medieval English word with no known morphologically exact cognates in other Germanic languages; did not gain distinct sense of "occultist, magic user" (as opposed to a philosopher or sage) until circa 1500s, aligning roughly with the starting English Renaissance. However, via Proto-Indo-European *weyd- cognate with Proto-Celtic *druwits (whence English druid), Proto-Slavic *vědьma (Polish wiedźma, Russian ве́дьма (védʹma)), Russian веду́н (vedún).

senses.d: Someone, usually male, who uses (or has skill with) magic, mystic items, and magical and mystical practices.
ex: The wizard conjured up a large fireball.
The wily wizard must be caught.

senses.d: One who is especially skilled or unusually talented in a particular field.
ex: He was a financial wizard, capable of predicting the movements of the stock markets.

senses.d: A computer program or script used to simplify complex operations, often for an inexperienced user.
ex: Use the "Add Network Connection" wizard to connect to a network in a series of simple steps.

senses.d: An administrator of a multi-user dungeon, or someone who has earned similar rights through gameplay; a user in wizard mode.
ex: It is certainly easy to believe the stories I hear of MUD wizards who demand deference and severely punish those who transgress […]
See how from far upon the eastern road / The star-led wizards [Magi] haste with odours sweet!

senses.d: A virgin over the age of 30 who does not socialize and thus cannot find a sexual partner.
Someone who deepfakes pornographic material using content from social media (usually selfies of people) at the request of others.

ex: "We had a wizard show," the young leader of an Australian squadron said, trying to keep the excitement out of his voice.
But he was a wizard flyer, that boy.
